sections.heading: Seeing you as you are
sections.text: Lord God Almighty, you know everything completely, and I cannot measure the depth of your wisdom. No one can stop your hand or push you out of your purposes. Nothing exists outside your care. Time does not limit you the way it limits me. Your power, mercy, wisdom, ways, and works are holy. Help me remember that I am speaking to the living God, not to an idea I can manage.
theological_themes: God's providential care over all things

scripture_references.connection: This passage praises God as both mighty and immeasurable in understanding, grounding the prayer's awe before God's infinite wisdom and power.
God declares that his purpose will stand and that he brings his will to pass, which supports the prayer's confession that no one can stop his hand.
The writer says all creatures are exposed before God, which fits the prayer's movement from worshiping God's greatness to standing honestly before him.

sections.heading: Owning the truth about my sin
sections.text: So how can I stand before you as though I am innocent? My sins are not few, and they are not small. I have loved what hides from your light. I have chased empty things as if they could save me. I have walked away from mercies you placed in my hands. I have treated your Son lightly, complained against your care, said the right words while my heart was far from you, and lived as though your covenant claims did not matter. If I am still here, it is because you are merciful.
theological_themes: human guilt before a holy God
misuse and neglect of God's mercies

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes fallen people as loving darkness rather than light because their works are evil, which directly supports the prayer's confession of preferring what hides from God.
This warning treats contempt for the Son and his blood as a grave sin, illuminating the prayer's severe language about treating Christ lightly.
In the middle of judgment and grief, the prophet confesses that God's people are not consumed because of his steadfast love and mercy, matching the prayer's hope that continued life is compassion.

sections.heading: Asking for repentance without despair
sections.text: Please lead me into real repentance. Do not let the sight of my sin drive me into hopelessness. Bring me to you with no excuses, no self-defense, and no pretending. Teach me to turn against my sin and judge it truthfully, while still trusting that your grace reaches even the worst sinner. I have nothing to bargain with. I come because you are merciful in Christ.
theological_themes: repentance as God's gift and work
grace for the chief of sinners
coming to God with no merit of one's own

scripture_references.connection: Paul distinguishes godly grief that leads to repentance from worldly grief that leads to death, which grounds the request to be brought to repentance without falling into despair.
Paul presents himself as the foremost sinner who received mercy, giving biblical shape to the prayer's confidence that grace reaches even the most guilty.

sections.heading: Looking at the cross honestly
sections.text: Bring me again to the cross. There, let me see what my sin really is and hate it instead of excusing it. Let me look at Jesus, the One my sin pierced, and understand that he was killed for me, and in a real sense, because of me. And do not let me insult his death by acting as if it might not be enough to save me. Teach me to trust the full worth of what he has done.
theological_themes: the cross reveals the evil of sin
confidence in the sufficiency of Christ's atonement

scripture_references.connection: This prophecy speaks of looking on the one who was pierced with mourning, which the New Testament connects to Christ's crucifixion and supports the prayer's call to see sin at the cross.
Peter teaches that Christ bore sins in his body on the tree so that his people might die to sin and live to righteousness, holding together substitution and moral transformation.
This passage emphasizes the decisive effectiveness of Christ's one offering, supporting the prayer's refusal to doubt whether his death is sufficient to save.

sections.heading: Learning from suffering and preparing for death
sections.text: When you call me to carry any cross, help me see that Jesus carried a heavier one before me and for me. In seasons of health, teach me not to live as though sickness cannot come. In bright days, make me ready for dark ones. While I am alive, prepare me to die faithfully, with my hope fixed on you.
theological_themes: bearing suffering in fellowship with Christ

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls his followers to deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow him, which grounds the prayer's language of bearing a cross under his lordship.
Believers are told to look to Jesus, who endured the cross, so that they will not grow weary; this supports comparing one's suffering with Christ's greater endurance.
Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days, which supports the prayer's desire to think wisely about sickness, darkness, and death before they arrive.

sections.heading: Resting in you through your Son
sections.text: Let my soul settle down in you, the immortal and holy God who is beyond me and yet has made yourself known. I do not have to guess what you are like, because you have shown yourself in the person and work of your Son. Thank you that Jesus is not ashamed to be known as the Friend of sinners. Let me rest in him.
theological_themes: confidence in the person and work of the Son

scripture_references.connection: Paul presents Christ as the image of the invisible God and the one through whom reconciliation is made by his blood, grounding the prayer's claim that God is revealed in the Son's person and work.
Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him for rest, which directly supports the prayer's longing for the soul to rest in God through Christ.
Though spoken as an accusation against Jesus, the title 'friend of sinners' reflects the scandal of his real welcome to the sinful and needy, which the prayer receives as hope.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase about coming to God while 'loathing myself' can be pastorally and theologically difficult. I rendered it as turning against and judging sin truthfully, rather than promoting self-hatred that would deny human dignity as God's image-bearer.
The phrase 'broken thy covenant' reflects a Puritan covenantal framework. I preserved the force as covenant unfaithfulness before God without specifying a debated covenant-theology system.

The line 'slain for me, and by me' uses strong devotional language about personal responsibility for Christ's death. I retained this as 'for me' and 'because of me,' while avoiding the implication that the praying person was historically present at the crucifixion.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated the opening claims about God's agency, time, and care as a combined confession of God's sovereignty, omniscience, holiness, and providence rather than separating them into abstract attributes.
I interpreted 'never despise his death by fearing its efficacy' as a warning against dishonoring Christ by doubting the sufficiency of his atonement for salvation.
I interpreted the final rest in God as rest specifically mediated through Christ, because the original grounds that rest in God as revealed in the person and work of the Son.
